summary: Joint Wolfsberg Group, ICC and BAFT guidance (2019 amendment) setting out Trade Finance Principles for managing financial crime risk in Documentary Credits, Bills for Collection, Guarantees/SBLCs, Open Account/Supply Chain Finance and FI Trade Loans. It defines core Trade-Based Money Laundering value-transfer techniques -- over-invoicing, under-invoicing, multiple invoicing, short/over shipping, obfuscation of goods type and phantom shipping -- describes sanctions, NPWMD and dual-use goods risks and the practical limitations FIs face in detecting them, and appends product-specific risk-indicator tables, including a glossary reference to funnel accounts used to layer trade-related payments.

By issuing more than one invoice for the same goods a seller can justify the receipt of multiple payments.

typologies.label: Third Party Payment Abuse

citations.quote: Unexplained Third Party: Person or entity that appears in a transaction or payment instruction where there has been no previous identification of that person or entity in the structure or documentation relating to the transaction.
Third parties are funding or part funding the DC value (just in time account credits to the settlement account)
Unexplained third parties
in the event that Party Y requests transfer of funds to an account with a bank not involved in the DC, that bank’s name should be subjected to screening by Bank A

typologies.review_justification: Found in Glossary 'Unexplained Third Party' (p.31); DC risk-indicator table (p.45); BC risk-indicator table (p.57); DC Stage 3 payment review (p.40). TBML008 describes settlement 'through a payer who is not the trade counterparty — an unrelated third party, split settlement, or a payment that does not match the trade... The payment breaks the link between the trade and the funds.' The advisory operationalises exactly this mechanism as bank controls: it defines an 'Unexplained Third Party' as one appearing in a transaction/payment instruction with no prior identification in the trade documentation, flags 'third parties funding or part funding the DC value' via just-in-time credits to the settlement account as a post-event red flag, and separately requires screening where a beneficiary directs payment to a bank not party to the original DC. Each of these is the same fact pattern TBML008 names: a payer/recipient disconnected from the documented trade counterparties, obscuring the true source or destination of funds.

typologies.label: Related Party Trading

citations.quote: Generally, these techniques rely upon collusion between the seller and buyer... The collusion may arise because both parties are controlled by the same persons.
Connected applicant and beneficiary
Connected Drawer or Drawee

typologies.review_justification: Found in Core Principles 3.1.iii (p.12); DC risk-indicator table (p.45); BC risk-indicator table (p.57). PAT009 identifies 'trading activity occurring between entities that are connected through ownership, control, directors, addresses, contacts or other network relationships.' The advisory's Core paper states plainly that value-transfer techniques such as over/under-invoicing rely on collusion that 'may arise because both parties are controlled by the same persons' — the same ownership/control nexus PAT009 targets — and then instantiates it as a standing red flag in both the DC table ('Connected applicant and beneficiary') and the BC table ('Connected Drawer or Drawee'), i.e. counterparties on opposite sides of the trade sharing common control, which is the network relationship PAT009 is built to surface.

typologies.label: Fraudulent Claims Under Standby/Guarantee Instruments

citations.quote: in the context of SBLCs and Guarantees, payments would generally be the exception. Risk controls specific to situations where Guarantees and SBLCs are drawn upon or paid should also address sanctions, expected activity and identify potential suspicious activity.
Claims made within a short time after issuance
Continuous claims under various guarantee instruments.
Claim pressure tactics

typologies.review_justification: Found in Appendix III, section 1.7 (p.60) and Risk Indicators table (p.67). No existing library typology addresses this mechanism (search returned no result above the score floor). The advisory develops a distinct technique specific to demand instruments: because SBLCs/Guarantees are non-performance undertakings where 'payments would generally be the exception,' any claim event is itself unusual, and the advisory groups three related indicators around abuse of that claim mechanism — claims made shortly after issuance (suggesting the instrument was never intended to support genuine performance), continuous claims across multiple guarantee instruments (a pattern of repeat extraction), and claim pressure tactics (coercive demand behaviour). This is a self-contained fraud mechanism — using the demand/default feature of a standby instrument to extract payment absent genuine non-performance — not covered by the TBML misrepresentation typologies already linked, which concern goods/invoice misstatement rather than the instrument's claim mechanism itself.

actors.name: Colluding Buyer and Seller
actors.role: Trade counterparties who collude to misrepresent the price, quantity or type of goods in trade documentation to move value outside an arm's-length transaction

citations.quote: Generally, these techniques rely upon collusion between the seller and buyer, since the intended outcome from such arrangements is obtaining a benefit in excess of what would be expected from an arm’s length transaction.

extraction_notes: This is an industry controls/guidance paper (Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT), not a case-specific advisory: it names no real actors, jurisdictions or transactions. The core TBML value-transfer methods (over/under invoicing, multiple invoicing, short/over shipping, obfuscation, phantom shipping) appear together in a single summary table (page 12) rather than being individually developed with worked examples, so those links are rated medium confidence; dual-use goods is discussed more extensively across the Core, Control Mechanisms and Challenges sections and is rated high. The document only states the publication year (2019), not a specific month or day, so published_on_precision is 'year'. No ISO country codes are stated anywhere in the text, so the jurisdictions list is left empty. Merged 3 reviewer addition(s) under schema 1.4.0; each carries its review_justification. Extraction-only record retained at data/records/.
